mainTopic: Rewriting a lost deed of sale: why the אחריות clause is left out, the danger of collecting twice, and whether a court writes a שובר
overview: This amud finishes a ברייתא about rewriting lost documents. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds that the court does not rewrite even a lost deed of sale. He also holds that if a gift recipient gives the deed back, the gift goes back, while the חכמים say the gift stays. The גמרא then asks why the first opinion rewrites a sale deed but leaves out its אחריות (guarantee) clause. רב ספרא explains that two guaranteed deeds for one field would let the buyer collect twice from the seller's other buyers. The גמרא objects that a creditor's loan document is torn after he collects, and it answers that the danger comes from someone claiming the field as his ancestors' land. רבינא explains why the buyer needs a scheme rather than simply collecting twice. Finally, the גמרא asks why the court does not give a full deed plus a cancellation note for the seller. The רבנן suggest this shows that courts do not write a שובר, and the response to them comes on the next amud.

steps.title: No replacement even for deeds of sale
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל rules that the court does not rewrite even a lost deed of buying and selling.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: The court does not write a replacement even for deeds of buying and selling.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with the opinion of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. He is stricter than the earlier opinion and says no replacement is written even for sale deeds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier opinion in the ברייתא allowed the court to rewrite a lost sale deed, just without the guarantee. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל goes further and says the court writes no replacement at all for a sale deed.

keyTerms.meaning: Deeds of buying and selling (sale documents for land)
We (the court) do not write
Even

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:

phrases.aramaic: אַף שִׁטְרֵי מִקָּח וּמִמְכָּר אֵין כּוֹתְבִין.
phrases.english: Even for deeds of buying and selling, we do not write [a replacement].
phrases.notes: The word "even" points back to the earlier opinion in the ברייתא, which did allow rewriting a sale deed.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: אַף שִׁטְרֵי מִקָּח וּמִמְכָּר אֵין כּוֹתְבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from the previous דף with a stricter opinion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, no replacement is written for a lost deed of sale.

steps.title: Returning a gift deed: does the gift go back?
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says that returning the gift deed returns the gift; the חכמים say the gift stays with the recipient.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבן שמעון בן גמליאל also used to say: If someone gives a gift of land to his friend, and the friend gave the deed back to him, the gift goes back. But the חכמים say: The gift stays where it is.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a second ruling of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, about a gift recipient who hands the deed back to the giver. The חכמים disagree with him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, handing back the deed counts as handing back the gift itself. The חכמים hold that the land was already acquired, so returning the paper does not undo the gift.

keyTerms.meaning: A gift
He returned the deed to him
His gift goes back (to the giver)
His gift stands (stays with the recipient)
The Sages (the majority opinion)

steps.whatToRemember: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: giving back the deed gives back the gift. חכמים: the gift stays.

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן הָיָה רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: And likewise Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel would say:
One who gives a gift to his fellow,
and he returned the deed to him —
phrases.notes: "He" here is the person who received the gift, giving the deed back to the giver.

phrases.english: his gift returns.
But the Sages say: his gift remains in place.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן הָיָה רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, related ruling of the same תנא, followed by the חכמים' disagreement.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: returning the gift deed returns the gift. חכמים: the gift remains.

steps.title: Why is the guarantee left out?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא's words "except for the guarantee in it" and asks for the reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: The court rewrites the sale deed, except for the guarantee in it. What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the earlier opinion in the ברייתא and asks why the replacement deed leaves out the guarantee clause. This sets up רב ספרא's explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sale deed usually includes אחריות, a promise that if the buyer loses the field to the seller's creditor, he may collect from the seller's other property. The ברייתא allowed a new deed but without that promise, and the גמרא wants to know why.

keyTerms.meaning: Guarantee clause: the seller's property backs up the sale if the field is taken away
What is the reason?

phrases.english: The Master said: Except for the guarantee that is in it.
phrases.notes: This quotes the earlier part of the ברייתא: a lost sale deed is rewritten, but without its guarantee clause.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: חוּץ מֵאַחְרָיוּת שֶׁבּוֹ. מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the ברייתא's text to analyzing one detail of the earlier opinion.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the court leaves out the guarantee clause when rewriting a lost sale deed.

steps.title: Two deeds could let the buyer collect twice
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא explains that the court never writes two deeds for one field, because a buyer holding two guaranteed deeds could collect from other buyers twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא said: Because we do not write two deeds for one field. Perhaps the seller's creditor will come and take the field from this buyer. The buyer will then bring out one deed and use its guarantee to take land from other buyers who bought from the seller. Then he will tell the creditor: "Keep quiet for now so I can settle into this land, and later come and take it from me." Then he will bring out the second deed and go take land from still other buyers.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא answers the question: with two guaranteed deeds, a buyer could pull off a trick and collect his loss two times.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each deed carries a guarantee, so each one can be used to collect from people who later bought land from the seller. The buyer works with the creditor so the field is taken from him twice, and he uses one deed each time. Leaving the guarantee out of the replacement deed blocks this trick.

keyTerms.meaning: Two deeds for one field
Creditor (here, a creditor of the seller)
Seizes or repossesses land for a debt
Buyers (here, people who later bought land from the same seller)
Keep quiet, hold off

steps.whatToRemember: The guarantee is left out so that one loss cannot be collected twice through two deeds.

phrases.english: Rav Safra said:
Because we do not write two deeds
for one field;
perhaps a creditor will go
and seize [the field] from this one,
phrases.notes: "This one" is the buyer who holds the two deeds.

phrases.english: and this one goes and takes out one [deed],
and seizes from buyers,
and says to the creditor:
"Keep quiet for me so that I can settle into it,
and then come and seize it from me."
And he takes out the other [deed],
and then goes again and seizes from other buyers.

steps.confusionAlert: The buyer is not seizing from the creditor. He uses each deed's guarantee to collect from other people who bought land from the same seller.
steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב סָפְרָא: לְפִי שֶׁאֵין כּוֹתְבִין שְׁנֵי שְׁטָרוֹת עַל שָׂדֶה אַחַת
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A second deed with a guarantee would let the buyer, working with the creditor, collect from later buyers twice.

steps.title: But the loan document was torn
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב ספרא: after the creditor collects once, his loan document is torn, so he has nothing to collect with a second time.
steps.simpleTranslation: But once the creditor collected, we tore up his loan document. With what would he seize the field a second time?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב ספרא's scenario and says it cannot actually happen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a creditor collects through the court, his loan document is torn so it cannot be used again. Without it, the creditor has no way to take the field back a second time, so the buyer's trick seems impossible.

keyTerms.meaning: We tore it
The loan document
With what?

phrases.english: But once we tore up the loan document,
phrases.notes: "We" means the court, which tears the loan document after the creditor collects the first time.

phrases.english: with what does he seize it again?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵיוָן דִּקְרַעְנֵיהּ לִשְׁטָרָא דְמַלְוֶה, בְּמַאי הָדַר טָרֵיף לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the scenario in step 4 is possible.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ספרא's scenario of the creditor seizing the field a second time
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: After the first collection the loan document is torn, so the creditor has no document to collect with again.

steps.title: The creditor's loan document must be torn
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא blocks the reply that the loan document was not torn. It cites רב נחמן: each court collection document is only valid if it states that the document before it was torn.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say we did not tear the loan document, that cannot be. רב נחמן said: any repossession document that does not say 'we tore the lender's loan document' is not valid. Any seizure document that does not say 'we tore the repossession document' is not valid. Any appraisal document that does not say 'we tore the seizure document' is not valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא strengthens its challenge from step 5. It shuts down the possible answer that maybe the creditor's loan document was never torn.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might defend רב ספרא by saying the creditor kept his loan document and could use it again. רב נחמן's rule shows the court always tears the old document at each stage of collection, and writes that it did so. So the creditor truly has nothing left to collect with a second time, and the challenge against רב ספרא stands.

keyTerms.meaning: A court document that lets a creditor take back land the debtor sold
A court document that lets the creditor track down and seize the debtor's property
Appraisal: a document setting the value of the property being collected
We tore it
And if you would say: introduces a possible answer that the גמרא is about to reject

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new topic. It is still the same challenge from step 5. The גמרא is closing a loophole so the question against רב ספרא stays strong.

phrases.english: And if you would say that we did not tear it,
But didn't Rav Naḥman say:
Any repossession document in which it is not written:
"We tore the lender's loan document"
is not a valid repossession document.
And any seizure document in which it is not written:
"We tore the repossession document"
is not a valid seizure document.
And any appraisal document in which it is not written:
"We tore the seizure document"
is not a valid appraisal document.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא דְּלָא קְרַעְנֵיהּ, וְהָא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reinforces the challenge of step 5 by blocking a possible defense of רב ספרא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ספרא's claim that a second guaranteed deed allows collecting twice (step 4).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every stage of court collection tears the previous document and records that it did. So the creditor cannot collect twice, and the buyer's second deed would never come into use.

steps.title: The danger comes from a claim of ancestral ownership
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב ספרא's worry is not about a creditor. It is about someone who takes the field back by proving it belonged to his ancestors. That kind of claim has no loan document to tear.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for a case where someone comes and takes the field based on the rights of his ancestors.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב ספרא. It changes the case: the person who takes the field from the buyer is not a creditor but an heir who says the land was his family's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An heir claiming his ancestors' land has no loan document, so nothing gets torn. He could take the field from the buyer again later. Each time, the buyer could use his guarantee to collect from the seller's other buyers, and with two deeds he could collect twice.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for: introduces a narrower case where the rule makes sense
Based on the rights of his ancestors, meaning he claims the land as his inheritance

steps.whyThisMatters: This saves רב ספרא's rule that the court never writes two guaranteed deeds for one field.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
for where someone comes based on the rights of his ancestors.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 5 and 6 by moving רב ספרא's concern to a different kind of claimant.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (a claimant through ancestors instead of a creditor)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב ספרא's concern was about a creditor, whose loan document gets torn, so double collection seemed impossible.
steps.terutzMaskana: The concern is an ancestral claimant. He has no document to tear, so the buyer could end up using two guaranteed deeds.

steps.title: Why did רב ספרא need such a complicated story?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא מדפתי asks רבינא why רב ספרא's case needed the buyer to ask the creditor to stay quiet. A buyer holding two deeds could simply collect twice on his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא מדפתי said to רבינא: Why does the buyer need to tell the creditor, 'Keep quiet about this land so I can become established in it'? Just say that since he holds two deeds, he collects and then collects again!
steps.whatsHappening: A new question is raised about how רב ספרא built his example. רב אחא מדפתי thinks a simpler case shows the same danger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ספרא described a scheme where the buyer and the creditor work together so the creditor collects twice. רב אחא מדפתי says this is unnecessary. Even if the field is taken only once, a buyer with two deeds could use each deed to collect from other buyers.

keyTerms.meaning: Keep quiet for me (about this matter)
And I will become established in it, meaning settled on the land
Let him derive it from: why not use a simpler reason?
He collects, and then collects again

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Aḥa of Difti said to Ravina:

phrases.aramaic: וּלְמָה לֵיהּ לְמֵימַר לֵיהּ לְבַעַל חוֹב:
phrases.english: And why does he need to say to the creditor:
"Keep quiet for me about this land, and I will become established in it"?
phrases.notes: This is the scheme from רב ספרא's case: the buyer asks the creditor to wait and come back later to collect again.

phrases.aramaic: תִּיפּוֹק לֵיהּ דְּכֵיוָן דְּנָקֵיט תְּרֵי שְׁטָרֵי –
phrases.english: Let him derive it from the fact that since he holds two deeds
he collects and then collects again!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא: וּלְמָה לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from defending רב ספרא's rule to questioning the details of the case he described.
steps.kashyaTarget: The scheme in רב ספרא's case, where the buyer asks the creditor to stay quiet.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two deeds alone would let the buyer collect twice, so the scheme with the creditor seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Too many people in court would expose the buyer
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that if the buyer collected twice on his own after only one loss, he would face too many opponents in court. His dishonesty would come out, so he needs the quieter scheme.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, he would have too many opponents in court against him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers רב אחא מדפתי and explains why רב ספרא needed the scheme.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the field was taken from the buyer only once, but he collects twice from other buyers, more people are suing each other than the facts explain. This would expose him. Only the scheme, where the creditor really takes the field a second time, gives him a believable reason to collect again.

keyTerms.meaning: They are many, too many
Litigants: opponents in a court case

steps.whatToRemember: רב ספרא's rule holds: the court does not write two guaranteed deeds for one field. The risk is real when the field is taken by an ancestral claimant. The scheme with the creditor is needed because simply collecting twice would draw too many opponents and expose the fraud.

phrases.english: If so,
he would have too many litigants against him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, נְפִישִׁי עֲלֵיהּ בַּעֲלֵי דִינִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אחא מדפתי's question from step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical reasoning (the simple fraud would be discovered)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Two deeds alone would let the buyer collect twice, so the scheme with the creditor seemed unnecessary.
steps.terutzMaskana: Collecting twice without a second real loss would bring too many opponents to court and expose him. So the realistic danger is the scheme with the creditor.

steps.title: Why not write a full deed plus a cancellation note for the seller?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a simpler fix. The court could write the buyer a full, proper deed and give the seller a cancellation note (תברא) declaring every other deed for this field invalid.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let the court write this buyer a proper deed, and write the seller a cancellation note that says: 'All documents that come out about this field are invalid, except the one that comes out on this date!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the need for a weaker replacement document. It suggests the court could give the buyer a full deed and protect the seller with a note that cancels every other deed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry until now was that the buyer might use two deeds to collect twice. A תברא in the seller's hand would solve that, because any second deed would be shown to be cancelled. So why does the buyer have to lose the full strength of his deed?

keyTerms.meaning: A proper, full-strength document (here, a deed of sale that includes a guarantee).
A cancellation note that declares other documents broken and invalid.
The seller.
On this date. This points to the one new deed written today.

phrases.english: But let them write for this one a proper document,
phrases.notes: "This one" is the buyer. A "proper" document is a full deed that includes the seller's guarantee.

phrases.english: and let them write a cancellation note for the seller:
'All documents that come out concerning this land

phrases.aramaic: – פְּסוּלִין, לְבַר מִן דְּיִפּוֹק בְּזִמְנָא דָּא״!
phrases.english: are invalid, except for the one that comes out on this date!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Steps 8-9 settled why the buyer needs a quiet scheme to collect twice. Now the גמרא offers a way to block double collection completely while still giving the buyer a full deed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that the buyer gets only a weaker document without full guarantee, which was explained by the fear of double collection.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the only danger is a second deed being used, a cancellation note in the seller's hand removes that danger. So there is no need to weaken the buyer's deed.

steps.title: This shows that the court does not write a receipt
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן, before רב פפא (some say before רב אשי), draw a conclusion. Since the ruling did not use the cancellation-note solution, it must hold that a court does not write a שובר.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן said this before רב פפא, and some say before רב אשי: This shows that we do not write a receipt.
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן answer the question by turning it into a lesson: the ruling chose not to use a cancellation note, so it must hold that courts do not write a שובר at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The suggestion in Step 10 only works if a court is willing to write a receipt or cancellation note for the seller. The ברייתא did not take that route, so the רבנן infer that its author holds a court does not write such a receipt. They say this before רב פפא (some say רב אשי), and his reaction comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: "This tells us": a phrase for drawing a lesson from a ruling.
A receipt saying a debt or claim has been paid or cancelled.

steps.whatToRemember: The רבנן suggest that the ברייתא did not use a full deed plus a cancellation note because its author holds that courts do not write a שובר. They say this before רב פפא (some say רב אשי), and his response comes on the next amud.
steps.confusionAlert: שובר and תברא are close in meaning here. Both are papers the seller keeps to cancel the buyer's other documents, so a rule against writing a שובר also blocks the תברא idea.
steps.whyThisMatters: Whether a court writes a שובר is a general question. This סוגיא draws evidence for it from a specific case.

phrases.english: The Rabbis said it before Rav Pappa,
and some say it was before Rav Ashi:
This tells us that we do not write a receipt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 10 by explaining why the cancellation-note solution was not used.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Inference from the ruling: the solution was not used because, by this view, courts do not write receipts.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The court could protect the seller with a תברא and give the buyer a full deed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The רבנן infer that the ברייתא holds a court does not write a שובר, which would explain why the buyer gets only the weaker document. The response before רב פפא (or רב אשי) continues on the next amud.
